title: GCP Core: Compute, GKE & IAM
summary: Master Google Cloud's project hierarchy, global VPCs, Compute Engine, GKE Standard vs Autopilot, Cloud IAM, and Cloud Storage — with a full AWS/Azure/GCP compare-and-contrast sheet for panel questions.
objectives: Navigate the GCP resource hierarchy and isolate environments with projects and named gcloud configurations
Build custom-mode VPCs and debug firewall rules through tag bindings
Run Compute Engine VMs cost-effectively with preemptibles and committed-use reasoning
Deploy GKE in Standard and Autopilot modes and grant pods storage access via Workload Identity
Map every AWS/Azure primitive from M41-M42 to its GCP equivalent for cross-cloud panel questions

notes.title: Projects and the Resource Hierarchy
notes.body: Everything in Google Cloud lives under a project, and projects nest under folders and an organization node. This hierarchy is not cosmetic: IAM policies and organization policies inherit downward, so a deny on the organization applies to every project beneath it. One project typically maps to one environment or application (billing-project-dev, billing-project-prod), which gives you per-project billing breakdowns and blast-radius isolation for free. Quotas are enforced per project per region — the GCP analogue of the Azure subscription quota you triaged in M41. The gcloud CLI scopes every command to a project: gcloud config set project my-proj, or per-command with --project. Worked example: a developer's gcloud compute instances list returns instances from the wrong environment. Diagnosis: gcloud config list shows core/project set to the prod project. Solution: gcloud config set project billing-project-dev, or better, use named configurations — gcloud config configurations create dev && gcloud config configurations activate dev — so switching environments is one command instead of editing config each time. The interview point: GCP's project model makes environment separation structural, where AWS leans on accounts and Azure on subscriptions/resource groups.

notes.title: VPC Networks and Firewall Rules
notes.body: A GCP VPC is global by default: one VPC spans all regions, and subnets are regional slices of it. This differs from AWS, where a VPC is regional and you peer across regions. Subnets have two modes: auto (a subnet per region created for you — fine for experiments, never for production) and custom (you define every subnet's CIDR — the production choice). Firewall rules in GCP are stateful and VPC-scoped, applied by tags or service accounts: e.g. allow tcp:443 from 0.0.0.0/0 to instances tagged web. There are no NACLs — one less layer than AWS. Implied rules exist: allow all egress, deny all ingress; your rules punch holes in the ingress deny. Worked example: a Compute Engine VM tagged 'api' serves nothing on port 8080 despite the app listening. Diagnosis: gcloud compute firewall-rules list shows no rule targeting tag 'api' for tcp:8080. Solution: gcloud compute firewall-rules create allow-api-8080 --allow tcp:8080 --target-tags api --source-ranges 10.0.0.0/8. Verify with gcloud compute firewall-rules describe allow-api-8080. The trap: creating the rule with --target-tags web while the instance is tagged api — the rule exists, matches nothing, and the firewall silently drops traffic. Always check the tag binding, not just the rule's existence.

notes.title: Compute Engine: VMs, Images, and Preemptibles
notes.body: Compute Engine VMs are built from images (public, custom, or machine images that bundle disks), shaped by machine types (e2-standard-4, n2, c2 for compute-heavy), and billed per second. Disks are persistent by default and independent of the VM, mirroring EBS semantics. Two GCP-specific concepts matter. First, preemptible VMs: up to deep discounts, terminable by Google with 30 seconds' notice — the GCP analogue of Spot, ideal for the same checkpointed batch work. Second, committed use discounts: 1- or 3-year commitments on steady capacity, the analogue of Reserved Instances/Savings Plans. Live migration keeps most VMs running through host maintenance, so reboots for maintenance are rarer than on other clouds. Worked example: list all running VMs across zones with their machine types: gcloud compute instances list --filter='status=RUNNING' --format='table(name,zone,machineType)'. To stop paying for an idle dev VM but keep its disk: gcloud compute instances stop my-dev-vm --zone us-central1-a — the disk persists and bills, the VM does not. The cost trap mirrors AWS: stopping is not deleting; disks, static IPs, and load balancer forwarding rules all bill independently. Audit monthly with gcloud compute disks list --filter='-users:*' to find orphaned disks.

notes.title: GKE: Standard vs Autopilot
notes.body: Google Kubernetes Engine comes in two modes. Standard mode: you manage the node pools (the direct analogue of AKS node pools and EKS node groups), choose machine types, and run the cluster autoscaler yourself. Autopilot: Google manages nodes, scaling, and security hardening — you declare workloads and pay per pod-requested resources, trading control for operational simplicity. Autopilot enforces opinions: no privileged pods, required resource requests, restricted host access. Workload Identity is GKE's IRSA equivalent: bind a Kubernetes ServiceAccount to a Google service account and pods get short-lived tokens with no keys — gcloud iam service-accounts add-iam-policy-binding with the workloadIdentityUser role. Worked example: create a standard cluster with two node pools: gcloud container clusters create il28-m43 --zone us-central1-a --machine-type e2-standard-4 --num-nodes 3, then gcloud container node-pools create batchpool --cluster il28-m43 --machine-type e2-standard-8 --preemptible --num-nodes 0 --enable-autoscaling --min-nodes 0 --max-nodes 10. The preemptible batch pool at min 0 mirrors the AKS spot-pool pattern from M41 exactly. The interview mapping to recite: node pools (AKS) = managed node groups (EKS) = node pools (GKE Standard); workload identity (AKS) = IRSA (EKS) = Workload Identity (GKE).

notes.title: Cloud IAM: Members, Roles, and Deny Policies
notes.body: Cloud IAM grants roles to members (users, groups, service accounts, domains) on resources, and permissions inherit down the hierarchy. Roles come in three flavors: basic (Owner/Editor/Viewer — broad, avoid in production), predefined (e.g. roles/compute.viewer — least-privilege friendly), and custom (your own permission sets). Service accounts are the non-human identities: every Compute Engine VM and every CI job should act as a service account, never as a user key — gcloud iam service-accounts keys create is the command you should almost never run, because keys are the leak vector. Prefer impersonation and workload identity federation instead. Deny policies (organization-level) let you write explicit denys, the GCP answer to AWS's explicit-Deny-wins rule. Worked example: a deploy service account needs to push images to Artifact Registry and nothing else. Solution: grant roles/artifactregistry.writer on the specific repository resource to the service account — not Editor on the project. Verify with gcloud projects get-iam-policy to audit bindings. The panel-ready contrast with AWS IAM: GCP binds roles to members per resource with inheritance; AWS attaches policies to users/groups/roles with explicit-Deny precedence. Both converge on the same practice: predefined narrow roles, service accounts for machines, no long-lived keys.

notes.title: Cloud Storage Classes and Lifecycle
notes.body: Cloud Storage buckets hold objects with the same four-class pattern as S3: Standard (hot), Nearline (read less than monthly), Coldline (read less than quarterly), Archive (yearly or less) — each step down cuts storage cost and raises retrieval cost and minimum durations (30/90/365 days). Autoclass automates transitions for unpredictable patterns, the analogue of S3 Intelligent-Tiering. Lifecycle rules in JSON transition or delete objects by age, and Object Versioning plus retention policies protect audit data. Buckets are global-named like S3; use gsutil or gcloud storage (the newer CLI): gcloud storage buckets create gs://my-bucket --location=us-central1 --storage-class=STANDARD. Worked example: the same 500 GB/month logs from M42, rarely read after a week, 1-year retention. Solution: lifecycle rule — SetStorageClass to NEARLINE at 30 days, to COLDLINE at 90 days, Delete at 365 days; enable versioning on the audit prefix. Verify: gcloud storage buckets describe gs://my-bucket --format=json | grep lifecycle. The cross-cloud trap: minimum storage durations — moving an object to Archive and deleting it at day 40 still bills 365 days. Lifecycle design must respect minimums or the 'savings' become a surcharge.

notes.title: Azure vs AWS vs GCP: The Compare-and-Contrast Sheet
notes.body: Panels ask you to compare clouds, so carry this sheet. Networking: AWS VPC is regional with IGW/NAT and SG+NACL; Azure VNet is regional with NSGs and route tables; GCP VPC is global with regional subnets and stateful firewall rules only. Identity: AWS IAM (users/roles/policies, explicit deny wins), Azure RBAC + Microsoft Entra (role assignments on scopes), GCP Cloud IAM (members/roles/resources with inheritance, deny policies). Compute: EC2 / Azure VMs / Compute Engine — all per-second billing, all with interruptible discounts (Spot / Spot VMs / preemptible). Kubernetes: EKS / AKS / GKE — managed control planes; node pools in all three; workload identity via IRSA / workload identity / Workload Identity. Object storage: S3 / Blob / Cloud Storage — hot-to-archive tiers with lifecycle automation in all three. The strategic point for M44: the primitives are 90% interchangeable, which is why Terraform can abstract them — the remaining 10% (IAM models, networking defaults, identity federation) is where multicloud gets expensive. Worked example: map the M42 lab to GCP — VPC becomes a custom-mode global VPC, the NAT Gateway becomes Cloud NAT, the IAM role becomes a service account with a predefined role, EKS+IRSA becomes GKE+Workload Identity, ALB becomes a global external HTTP(S) load balancer. If you can narrate that mapping, you can work on any cloud.

cards.front: GCP resource hierarchy order (top to bottom)
cards.back: Organization -> folders -> projects -> resources; IAM and organization policies inherit downward

cards.front: How do you switch gcloud between dev and prod cleanly?
cards.back: Named configurations: gcloud config configurations create dev / activate dev — never hand-edit core/project per command

cards.front: GCP VPC: global or regional? Subnets?
cards.back: VPC is global; subnets are regional. (AWS VPCs are regional.) Use custom subnet mode in production, never auto mode
Rules bind via --target-tags or service accounts; a rule with the wrong tag matches nothing and traffic is silently dropped. Check the binding, not just the rule

cards.front: Command: create a firewall rule for tcp:8080 to instances tagged 'api'
cards.back: gcloud compute firewall-rules create allow-api-8080 --allow tcp:8080 --target-tags api --source-ranges 10.0.0.0/8

cards.front: GCP's analogue of AWS Spot instances
cards.back: Preemptible VMs — deep discount, 30-second termination notice; use for checkpointed batch, never for databases
Standard: you manage node pools, machine types, autoscaler. Autopilot: Google manages nodes/security; you pay per pod requests; privileged pods restricted
Workload Identity: bind a Kubernetes ServiceAccount to a Google service account; pods get short-lived tokens, no keys

cards.front: Command you should almost never run (GCP keys)
cards.back: gcloud iam service-accounts keys create — long-lived keys are the leak vector; use impersonation or workload identity federation

cards.front: Cloud Storage classes in access-frequency order
cards.back: Standard -> Nearline (monthly) -> Coldline (quarterly) -> Archive (yearly); minimum durations 30/90/365 days
EKS IRSA = AKS workload identity = GKE Workload Identity: short-lived tokens mapping K8s service accounts to cloud roles
Primitives are ~90% interchangeable (Terraform abstracts them); the costly 10% is IAM models, networking defaults, and identity federation

quiz.q: A gcloud command lists instances from the wrong environment. Fastest correct fix?
choices: gcloud config configurations activate dev (use named configurations per environment)
quiz.explain: The active configuration's core/project selects the project. Named configurations make environment switching one command and prevent prod/dev mix-ups.

quiz.q: Why is a GCP VPC described as global while an AWS VPC is regional?
choices: One GCP VPC spans all regions with regional subnets; AWS VPCs live in one region and peer across regions
quiz.explain: GCP VPCs are global constructs; subnets are the regional slices. AWS VPCs are regional, so cross-region traffic needs peering or Transit Gateway.

quiz.q: A firewall rule allows tcp:8080 with --target-tags web, but the VM is tagged api and serves nothing. Cause?
choices: The rule's target tag does not match the VM's tag, so the rule matches nothing
quiz.explain: Tag binding is exact: the rule exists but selects zero instances. Always verify the target binding, not just the rule's existence.

quiz.q: Which workload belongs on preemptible VMs?
choices: A checkpointed nightly batch job that tolerates restarts
A stateful message queue with no replication
quiz.explain: Preemptibles can die with 30 seconds' notice — only fault-tolerant, checkpointed batch work qualifies. Stateful singletons never do.

quiz.q: A team wants managed Kubernetes but refuses to manage node pools. Which GKE mode?
quiz.explain: Autopilot manages nodes, scaling, and hardening; you pay per pod-requested resources and accept its security opinions (no privileged pods).

quiz.q: A GKE pod needs to read from Cloud Storage with no keys. What do you configure?
choices: A service account key mounted as a secret
Workload Identity: bind the K8s ServiceAccount to a Google service account with storage.objectViewer
quiz.explain: Workload Identity issues short-lived tokens via OIDC — the GKE equivalent of IRSA. Keys in secrets are the pattern this replaces.

quiz.q: Logs move to Archive class but are deleted after 40 days. What happens to the bill?
choices: Archive has a 365-day minimum — you are billed for the full minimum despite early deletion
quiz.explain: Minimum storage durations (Nearline 30, Coldline 90, Archive 365 days) mean early deletion still bills the minimum. Lifecycle rules must respect them.

quiz.q: Map the AWS M42 lab to GCP: NAT Gateway becomes?
quiz.explain: Cloud NAT provides managed outbound NAT for private subnets — the direct analogue of the AWS NAT Gateway in the lab.

quiz.q: In the compare-and-contrast sheet, what is the costly 10% of multicloud?
choices: IAM models, networking defaults, and identity federation
quiz.explain: Compute and storage primitives are interchangeable; identity models, network defaults, and federation are where multicloud complexity and cost concentrate.

items.prompt: Command: list running Compute Engine VMs as a table of name, zone, machine type.
items.explain: Filter plus table format — the two flags that turn a dump into triage output.

items.prompt: Command: create a firewall rule allowing tcp:8080 to tag 'api' from 10.0.0.0/8.
items.answer: gcloud compute firewall-rules create allow-api-8080 --allow tcp:8080 --target-tags api --source-ranges 10.0.0.0/8
items.explain: Name, allow, target-tags, source-ranges — and verify the tag matches the instances.

items.prompt: Your firewall rule exists but traffic is dropped. First check?
items.answer: Whether the rule's target tags/service accounts actually match the instances.
items.explain: A rule that selects nothing is the silent killer — check bindings before ports.

items.prompt: Command: create a GKE cluster with 3 e2-standard-4 nodes.
items.answer: gcloud container clusters create il28-m43 --zone us-central1-a --machine-type e2-standard-4 --num-nodes 3
items.explain: Standard mode; add a preemptible autoscaled node pool next for batch.

items.prompt: Command: add a preemptible batch node pool, min 0 max 10.
items.answer: gcloud container node-pools create batchpool --cluster il28-m43 --machine-type e2-standard-8 --preemptible --num-nodes 0 --enable-autoscaling --min-nodes 0 --max-nodes 10
items.explain: Mirrors the AKS spot-pool pattern: cheap interruptible capacity scaled to zero.
Disks bill independently of VMs — this filter finds the money leaks.

items.answer: GKE Workload Identity, AKS workload identity (federated credentials), EKS IRSA.
items.explain: Same pattern, three names — short-lived tokens, no keys, K8s SA mapped to cloud role.

items.prompt: AWS VPC is regional; GCP VPC is ___; subnets are ___.
items.explain: Say it as the contrast — panels test whether you carry both models.

items.prompt: Map: AWS security group + NACL -> GCP ___; Azure NSG -> GCP ___.
items.answer: GCP stateful firewall rules (no NACL equivalent); same — GCP firewall rules.
items.explain: GCP collapses the two AWS layers into one stateful rule set.
Interruptible discounts exist on all three; names differ.
Unknown-pattern automation on both; S3 names it Intelligent-Tiering, GCP Autoclass.

items.prompt: Map: EKS managed node group -> AKS ___ -> GKE Standard ___.
items.explain: All three converged on the node-pool concept — say the trio.

items.prompt: Biggest IAM model difference: AWS vs GCP?
items.answer: AWS attaches policies to identities with explicit-deny precedence; GCP binds roles to members per resource with hierarchy inheritance (+ deny policies).
items.explain: One sentence each — this is the panel-ready contrast.

items.prompt: When does the 90/10 rule say multicloud is worth it?
items.answer: Rarely for the primitives (90% interchangeable); justified by the 10%: regulatory, data gravity, or best-of-breed service needs — decided deliberately, not by accident.
items.explain: Leads into M44: multicloud is a strategy decision with a cost model, not a default.

handsOnLab.title: Lab: GCP VPC, GKE with Workload Identity, and the cross-cloud map
handsOnLab.brief: You will build a custom-mode VPC, deploy GKE Standard with a preemptible batch pool, give a pod Cloud Storage access through Workload Identity with no keys, and document the AWS/Azure/GCP mapping. Use the GCP free tier where possible and delete everything after.
steps: Create the project (or pick a lab project) and set it: gcloud projects create il28-m43-lab --name='IL28 M43'; gcloud config set project il28-m43-lab. Create dev/prod named configurations.

Create a custom-mode global VPC: gcloud compute networks create vpc-m43 --subnet-mode=custom; add two regional subnets: gcloud compute networks subnets create subnet-a --network vpc-m43 --region us-central1 --range 10.2.0.0/20.
Add a firewall rule allowing SSH from your IP to tagged instances, and confirm gcloud compute firewall-rules list shows the correct target tags.
Create the GKE cluster: gcloud container clusters create il28-m43 --zone us-central1-a --machine-type e2-standard-4 --num-nodes 2 --network vpc-m43 --subnetwork subnet-a.

Add the preemptible batch pool: gcloud container node-pools create batchpool --cluster il28-m43 --machine-type e2-standard-8 --preemptible --num-nodes 0 --enable-autoscaling --min-nodes 0 --max-nodes 6 --node-taints batch=true:NoSchedule.
Create a Cloud Storage bucket with a lifecycle JSON (Nearline at 30d, Coldline at 90d, delete at 365d) and upload a test object with gcloud storage cp.
Create a Google service account with roles/storage.objectViewer on the bucket; enable Workload Identity on the cluster; bind the K8s ServiceAccount to it via the workloadIdentityUser IAM binding.
Deploy a test pod using that ServiceAccount that runs gcloud storage ls gs://<bucket>; confirm it lists objects with no keys in the pod.
Taint-check: deploy a pod without the batch toleration and confirm it never lands on batchpool nodes; add the toleration and watch it schedule when you scale batchpool.
Write the cross-cloud map: one row each for networking, identity, interruptible compute, managed K8s, object storage, and L7 load balancing across AWS/Azure/GCP.

Delete everything: gcloud container clusters delete il28-m43 --zone us-central1-a --quiet; delete the bucket with gcloud storage rm -r; delete subnets, firewall rules, and the VPC; verify with gcloud compute networks list.
Record the cost: check the billing console for the day's spend and note which resources billed while idle.
handsOnLab.deliverable: A (then deleted) custom-mode VPC, a GKE cluster with a preemptible tainted batch pool, a pod reading Cloud Storage via Workload Identity with zero keys, and a written AWS/Azure/GCP mapping table.
handsOnLab.checkpoint: The pod lists bucket objects with no keys present; the batch pool scales from 0 under load; gcloud compute networks list shows no lab VPC after teardown.

mockTask.q: A GKE pod needs read access to a Cloud Storage bucket. Which approach is correct?
choices: Create a service account key and mount it as a Kubernetes secret
Workload Identity: bind the pod's ServiceAccount to a Google service account holding storage.objectViewer on the bucket
Give the node pool's service account Project Owner
mockTask.explain: Workload Identity issues short-lived OIDC tokens with no keys to leak or rotate, scoped to exactly the needed role on the bucket. Keys in secrets, public buckets, and Owner grants all fail least privilege.
